sections.h2: Dry cooling uses far less water per kWh, even counting the power plant

chart.title: Dry cooling saves about 88% of the water once the power plant's share counts
chart.sub: Litres per kWh of IT load; tower at 3 cycles of concentration.
chart.source: This blog's arithmetic on ECBC 2017 minimums; NTPC 2023-24.
chart.accent: Dry cooling, water at power plant
rows: Dry cooling, water at power plant

sections.means: Counting the power plant's water, dry cooling uses about 0.27 litres per kWh against about 2.2 for an evaporative tower.
sections.todo: Use dry cooling where water is scarce, and set its design temperature high enough to avoid compressors on most hours.

sections.h2: The price of dry cooling is electricity, and the worst case is avoidable

chart.title: Air-cooled chillers need 0.33 kWh to remove a kWh of heat, against 0.20 for water-cooled
chart.sub: Electricity per kWh of heat removed, tower fans and pumps included.
chart.source: India's Energy Conservation Building Code (2017), minimum efficiencies.

sections.means: Dry cooling with compressors on every hour adds 0.135 kWh per kWh of IT load, which is the worst case the post costs out.
sections.todo: Keep closed-loop air-cooled chillers in existing halls and raise supply temperatures rather than converting to towers.

sections.h2: Coastal campuses sit at cable landings, while inland ones are hundreds of km away

chart.title: Four campuses sit within 29 km of a cable landing; the rest are 478 km or more away
chart.sub: Great-circle distance from each campus to its nearest subsea cable landing.
chart.source: This blog's arithmetic on city-centre coordinates; cable landings per the post.

sections.means: Coastal sites can cool a closed inner loop through seawater, which the post calls the efficient answer on the coast.
sections.todo: Build coastal campuses with closed inner loops, and never cool with municipal drinking water.
